```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
ri <- function(x) knitr::inline_expr(x)
```

This article is for authors whose prose cannot call R: a Quarto document on
the Jupyter or Julia engine, a plain Pandoc document, or a chapter built
from a values file. It assumes you know `vignette("values", package =
"weft")` and `vignette("wording", package = "weft")`. After it you will be
able to publish a value from R, Python or Julia, write it in a sentence by
name, say what the resolver does with it, and know what fails and what is
not built yet.

None of the code in this article is run when the article is built. The
output shown was produced by running it.

## A name instead of an R expression

A named value is a code span that holds one name, directly followed by an
attribute block with a weft class: `` `depth`{.num} ``. Code publishes a
value under that name. When the document renders, a Pandoc filter replaces
the span with the value, formatted by the class.

`````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
---
title: "Creek survey"
---

````{.weft-values}
{"weft":1,"values":{"depth":{"t":"float","v":"3.14159"},"n_high":{"t":"int","v":"1"}}}
````

Mean depth was `depth`{.num digits="2"} m.
[No site | One site | # sites]{n="n_high"} read above the trigger.
`````

That document needs no R, no Python and no Julia. It renders as:

```text
Mean depth was 3.14 m. One site read above the trigger.
```

The block in the middle is how code hands a value over. You rarely write one
by hand: `weft_put()` in R, `put()` in Python and `@put` in Julia write it for
you. A name is ASCII letters, digits, `_` and `.`, starting with a letter or
`_`, and at most 64 characters. A dot is part of the name: `n.sites` is one
name, and there is no `site.depth` that reaches into a value. A name cannot
be `TRUE`, `FALSE`, `True`, `False`, `true`, `false`, `NA`, `NULL`, `None`,
`nothing`, `missing`, `Inf` or `NaN`.

`.val` prints a named value as it is: the digits of an integer, the shortest
text of a float, a decimal as written, a string, an ISO date, `true` or
`false`. It takes no wording class. A float prints in one form whatever
language wrote it: `100000`, not `100000.0`, and `1e+23`, as R writes it.
Published text is data, not markdown, so `.val` with a text or collapse class
(`.cap`, `.and`) prints a `*` or a `<` in a string as it is.

### When to write a name

- In a document that is not knit, write names. The document is on the
  Jupyter engine, the Julia engine, the markdown engine or plain Pandoc, so
  no R runs to evaluate an expression.
- In a knitr document (an `.Rmd`, or a `.qmd` with `engine: knitr`), keep
  writing R expressions. R values and spans stay R. Write a name where the
  hooks cannot reach: text a chunk prints with `results: asis`, a caption on
  a chunk that is cached or not evaluated, or a value from Python or Julia
  that must print exactly.

A named value means the same in every document and on every engine.

## Publishing from R

In a knitr document you usually publish nothing. When the source holds a
named value, weft publishes every name it uses that is bound in the knit and
has changed, at the start of each block of prose and at the end of the
document:

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
---
title: "Creek survey"
output: md_document
knitr:
  opts_knit:
    weft: !expr weft::weft_setup()
---

```{r setup, include = FALSE}
turbidity <- c(Upper = 4.2, Middle = 7.9, Lower = 12.6)
worst <- max(turbidity)
n_high <- sum(turbidity > 10)
```

The worst reading was `worst`{.num} NTU.
[No site | One site | # sites]{n="n_high"} read high.
````

Automatic publishing applies only when the source holds at least one named
value. A governor name alone, such as `if="rising"`, does not switch it on.

`weft_put()` publishes by hand. Use it for text a chunk prints with
`results = "asis"`, for a value that carries a check, and for a chunk with no
value of its own to show:

```r
weft_put(n_sites = length(turbidity))      # a name and a value
weft_put(worst, n_high)                    # variables, under their own names
weft_put(limit = claim(50, . > 10))        # the check travels with the value
```

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
```{r, results = "asis"}
weft_put(n_sites = length(turbidity))
cat("We sampled `n_sites`{.word} sites.\n")
```
````

In a chunk with `results = "asis"` the block is written at once, so the text
printed after it sees the name. Otherwise the names wait and go out before
the next block of prose. A chunk with `include: false` therefore still
publishes under knitr.

`weft_put()` takes named arguments, or bare variable names. It accepts a
bool, a whole or decimal number, a string, a factor, a `Date`, an `integer64`
or an atomic vector of these, up to 10,000 elements. `NA`, `NaN`, `Inf` and
`NULL` publish as missing. A value with units is refused. Any other object,
such as a data frame, a list, a complex number or a raw vector, publishes as
an error that is reported where the name is used.

A named vector of length 1 publishes as a list of one, with its name as the
key, as a longer named vector does. Under a scalar class the filter prints a
list of exactly one element as that element, so `.num` works on it and
`.pairs` keeps the name:

```r
weft_put(worst = c(Upper = 12.6))
```

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
The worst reading was `worst`{.pairs}.
````

```text
The worst reading was Upper (12.6).
```

## Text a chunk prints

A chunk with `results = "asis"` that prints sentences, one per site or one
per model, writes text that knitr's hooks never see as prose. Typing the
numbers into that text with `paste()` or `sprintf()` loses every check.
There are two ways to keep them, and they print the same.

**`weft_str()`** resolves the markup in R, at once, and returns markdown.
Its constructs are R expressions, so units, the dictionary and project
formatters all work:

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
```{r, results = "asis"}
cat(weft_str("We sampled [a site | # sites]{n=\"n_sites\"}, mean `r mean_ntu`{.num} NTU."), "\n")
```
````

**A named value** leaves the markup for the filter. Publish the values
first, then print text that names them:

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
```{r, results = "asis"}
weft_put(n_sites, mean_ntu)
cat("We sampled [a site | # sites]{n=\"n_sites\"}, mean `mean_ntu`{.num} NTU.\n")
```
````

Both print:

```text
We sampled 3 sites, mean 8.2 NTU.
```

Under `weft_str()` a failed check, a missing value or a value error is
collected as it is in prose and marked with the chunk that printed it. A
named value is checked by the filter, so its text keeps to the filter's
grammar (no units, no R expressions), but a check given to `weft_put()`
travels with the value and counts each time the name is used. Use
`weft_str()` for text that needs R; use a name when the same text also
comes from Python or Julia, or from a values file.

## Publishing from Python

For a notebook on the Jupyter engine, install the Python package in the
Python Quarto uses. The distribution is `weft-prose`; the module is `weft`:

```
pip install "git+https://github.com/vorpalvorpal/weft#subdirectory=inst/python"
```

```python
from weft import put, auto, claim
```

`put()` publishes names. A cell that calls it shows nothing to the reader; the
filter removes the block it prints. Hide the code with `echo: false`.

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
---
title: "Creek survey"
jupyter: python3
---

```{python}
#| echo: false
from decimal import Decimal
from weft import put
depth = 3.14159
sites = ['Upper', 'Lower', 'Weir']
big = 2**70
price = Decimal('0.10')
put(depth=depth, sites=sites, big=big, price=price)
```

Mean depth was `depth`{.num digits="2"} m at `sites`{.and}.
The count was `big`{.val} and the price `price`{.num digits="2"}.
````

It renders as:

```text
Mean depth was 3.14 m at Upper, Lower and Weir. The count was
1180591620717411303424 and the price 0.10.
```

`put(depth=depth)`, `put({'n.sites': 4})` and a mix of the two are all
accepted. A name that is not a name raises `PublishError`, and nothing is
published from that call.

`auto()` publishes for you. Call it once, in an early cell:

```python
from weft import auto
auto()
```

After each cell, `auto()` publishes the names the document uses that the cell
changed. It reads the document's source from Quarto's environment, or from a
path you give it: `auto("report.qmd")`. Call it in a cell that has output.
A cell with `include: false` or `output: false` publishes nothing on this
engine.

`auto()` has the same gate as R's automatic publishing. It publishes only when
the source holds at least one named value, and a governor name alone, such as
`if="rising"`, does not switch it on. A list of more than 10,000 elements
raises an error from `auto()`, as it does from `put()`; no error record is
published.

In a knitr document (an `.Rmd`, or a `.qmd` with `engine: knitr`), `put()` and
`auto()` in a Python chunk, and `put` and `@put` in a Julia chunk, hand their
names to R. R writes them as one block before the next block of prose, as
`weft_put()` does, and nothing is printed in the chunk. A chunk with
`include: false` still publishes. Under knitr, `auto()` publishes the names
the source uses that are bound in Python's `__main__`. Julia has no `auto()`.

## Publishing from Julia

Julia has `put` and `@put`:

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
---
title: "Creek survey"
engine: julia
---

```{julia}
#| echo: false
using Weft
depth = 3.14159
n_high = 1
@put depth n_high
```

Mean depth was `depth`{.num digits="2"} m.
[No site | One site | # sites]{n="n_high"} read above the trigger.
````

`@put a b` publishes each variable under its own name. `Weft.put(depth=3.14159)`
and `Weft.put(:depth => 3.14159)` publish a name and a value. Julia has no
`auto()`.

## Set-up

On the engines, three things must be in place: weft's filter in the project,
the Python or Julia package in the language the notebook uses, and, for the
gate and `verify()`, R with weft installed.

**Quarto project.** Run `weft::use_quarto()`. It writes the extension
`_extensions/weft-check/`, which holds the filters `weft.lua` and
`weft-check.lua` and the folder `weftlib/`, and names it under `filters:` in
`_quarto.yml`. `weft.lua` runs first. The extension also holds
`weft-output.lua`, the rendered-output check, which `_quarto.yml` names by
its path to run after Quarto's own filters (see `vignette("gate", package =
"weft")`). `use_quarto()` also prints the install
line for the language packages when the project has a document that needs
them.

**R Markdown.** Run `weft::use_setup()`. For an `.Rmd` outside a Quarto
project it copies `weft.lua`, `weft-check.lua`, `weft-output.lua` and
`weftlib/` beside the document and names them in `pandoc_args`. A document
set up before named values that names only `weft-check.lua` gets `weft.lua`
added before it, and one set up before the rendered-output check gets
`weft-output.lua` added last.

**Python.** The pip line above. `weft::status()` gains a `python` row when
the project has a Jupyter-engine document, and says whether `import weft`
runs in the Python Quarto would use. Under knitr you need no pip install: R
loads its own copy of the package from weft.

**Julia.** `using Weft` has to find the package. The line `use_quarto()`
prints is:

```julia
using Pkg; Pkg.add(url = "https://github.com/vorpalvorpal/weft", subdir = "inst/julia/Weft")
```

Setting `JULIA_LOAD_PATH` in your shell does not help, because the notebook
worker that Quarto starts does not inherit it. The `julia:` key in
`_quarto.yml` does reach the worker. To use the copy that ships with the R
package, point the worker at it:

```yaml
engine: julia
julia:
  env: ["JULIA_LOAD_PATH=/path/to/library/weft/julia:"]
```

The path is `system.file("julia", package = "weft")` in R. The trailing
separator (`:`, and `;` on Windows) keeps Julia's own default load path.
This is how weft's own tests make `using Weft` work on the engine. Under
knitr you need nothing: R puts the package on the load path itself.

R is still needed on a machine that runs the commit gate, `lints()`, or
`verify()`, even for a project with no R code.

## What the filter resolves

`weft.lua` resolves named values wherever they are. In a document that is not
knit it resolves every weft construct. In a knitr document it resolves named
values and any span that reaches Pandoc still carrying a governor.

It implements the number, wording, collapse and text classes: `.num`, `.pct`,
`.val`, `.sci`, `.p`, `.date`, `.plus`, `.no`, `.word`, `.count`, `.ord`,
`.and`, `.or`, `.pairs`, `.range`, `.ul`, `.ol`, `.dl`, `.a`, `.cap`,
`.strong`, `.em`; the keys `digits`, `sigfig`, `label` (on `.p`), `sep`,
`last`, `trunc`, `none`; the governors `if`, `n`, `sign` and `list`, ids and
back-references; `cite` spans; and `decision` on a `cite` span or a
`.weft-literal`, which it removes from the output. It reads the settings
`p_digits` and `p_label`. A float prints as R prints it. An integer or a decimal prints exactly,
whatever its size.

### Where the filter's grammar differs from R's

On the R path the value of `if` is any R expression. In the filter it is
smaller, and everything else is an error. A condition is:

- a name whose value is a bool, or `!` directly before such a name, or
- one comparison `a OP b`, where `OP` is `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `==` or `!=`,
  and each side is a name, a number such as `10` or `1.5`, or a
  single-quoted string such as `'north'`, with at least one side a name.

Conditions are joined by commas, as on the R path.

```markdown
[above | within]{if="worst > limit"}
[a gap | no gap]{if="n_gap > 10, n_sites >= 3"}
[north | south]{if="region == 'north'"}
[the backlog cleared | the backlog grew]{if="n_open < 5, !paused"}
[before | after]{if="sampled < '2026-07-01'"}
```

`!` applies to one bool name only. `!paused` is true when `paused` is false.
`!!a`, `!a == b` and `!(a)` are construct errors, because R and Julia read
`!a > b` differently. A one-arm guard can use it too:
`[Sampling ran on schedule]{if="!delayed"}` fails when `delayed` is true.

Numbers compare exactly, as decimals. A float is compared by its shortest
text, so `0.1` is equal to the decimal `0.1` and to the literal `0.1`. Strings
compare with `==` and `!=` only. Dates compare in calendar order. A date
compares with a string literal that is a valid `YYYY-MM-DD` date, on either
side of the operator, in calendar order. Any other string literal, an
impossible date such as `'2026-02-30'`, or a string name is a value error.
A bool is not truthy: `0`, `""` and a list of one bool are errors, not false.

There are no arbitrary expressions. `worst + 1 > 3`, `len(x) > 2`, `a && b`,
`0 < x < 1` and `3 > 2` are construct errors. The fix is always the same:
compute it in code and publish the result under a name.

Governor values are also names. `n` takes a name, `.` or `#id`. `sign` takes
a name or `#id`. `list` takes a name. A governor value that starts with a
space, such as `n=" k"`, is a construct error. Pandoc does not read such a
value as an attribute, so the span would print as text.

More differences:

- Units (`.uname`, `.usym`, `.nounit`, and the key `unit=` on a named value or
  on an `n`, `sign` or `list` span) and project formatters are not available.
  They fail loudly and never print the raw value.
- `.num`, `.pct`, `.sci` and `.p` on a list with no collapse class print each
  element, joined by a comma and a space, as R does: `` `depths`{.num} ``
  prints `1.3, 3.5`. A list of strings under one of these classes is a value
  error.
- `date_format` reads the tokens `%d`, `%-d`, `%e`, `%m`, `%-m`, `%B`, `%b`,
  `%A`, `%a`, `%Y`, `%y`, `%j` and `%%`, and literal text, in English. With
  `date_format: "%A %-d %B %Y"` a `.date` prints `Thursday 29 February 2024`.
  Any other token, such as `%U` or `%H`, is a value error that says it is not available.
- `.ord`, `.word`, `.count`, `.range` and the `n` and `sign` governors work from
  the exact digits of an integer. `.ord` of 9007199254740993 prints
  `9,007,199,254,740,993rd`, with no rounding past 2^53.
- Order matters. A construct sees the latest value published above it. A
  name used above every publication of it takes the value published below,
  when there is exactly one (see "A name used above its value" below).
  Captions and the front-matter fields `title`, `subtitle`, `abstract` and
  `description` see each name's last published value, so a named value works
  in any caption on any chunk. A named value in another front-matter field is
  a failure that says the filter does not resolve that field.
- A named value in an arm that is not chosen is never read.

### Richer conditions: publish a bool

A condition the filter reads is a comparison of a name against a name or a
literal, with one of six operators: `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `==` and `!=`. A
bool name on its own, or with `!` before it, is a condition too. For
anything richer, compute it in code and publish the answer as a bool:

```python
put(all_rising=all(s > 0 for s in slopes), in_band=6.5 <= do_mean <= 8.5)
```

```r
weft_values_write("_weft/values/survey.json",
                  all_rising = all(trend$slope > 0),
                  in_band = in_range(do_mean, dict$do_band))
```

```markdown
[All]{if="all_rising"} sites rose, and the mean was
[within | outside]{if="in_band"} the band.
```

The code that computes the bool is where the reasoning lives, and it can be
read and tested there. In a knitr document none of this is needed: an `if`
span takes any R expression.

## A name used above its value

A summary at the top of a document often states a value that a chunk
further down computes. A named value can be used above the code that
publishes it, provided the name takes exactly one value in the document:

````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
In summary, `n_sites`{.count} sites were sampled.

```{r}
n_sites <- nrow(sites)
```
````

The filter looks ahead, finds the one value published under `n_sites`, and
prints it. This works on every engine, in knitr documents too. Several
publications count as one value when they agree: a `weft_put()` in a loop
that publishes the same value each time, or a values file and a block that
agree. A missing value counts as a value.

When the document publishes different values under the name below the use,
the filter cannot tell which one the sentence means, and the render fails:

```text
weft: 1 failure
  b.md:1  [no value] `n`{.count}
      `n` is used above its first publication, and the document publishes 2 different values for it below; a use above every publication needs a name that takes one value (rule 1.12.7).
      Move the sentence below the value it means, or publish that value under a name of its own.
```

A use below a publication is unchanged: it takes the latest value above it.

Inline R is not covered. `` `r ri("n_sites")` `` above the chunk is
evaluated where it stands, before `n_sites` exists. When it fails with
"object not found", the hint says to write it as a named value instead.

One trap is left under knitr. If you render with `rmarkdown::render()` in
an interactive session that still holds an old `n_sites` in the global
environment, the hooks publish that old value at the first block of prose,
so the sentence is no longer above every publication and prints the old
value. Render in a fresh R session, as the Knit button and `quarto render`
do.

## Checks

A check made where code runs counts there. In Python, `claim(x, "> 10")`
returns `x` and raises when the check fails; a string that starts with a
comparison operator applies to the value, and any other string is an
expression in which `_` is the value:

```python
from weft import claim
n = claim(n, "> 10")
even = claim(n, "_ % 2 == 0")
depth = claim(depth, "> 0", "< 50", level="warn")   # record, and go on
```

In Julia the check is an expression, and `_` stands for the value:

```julia
using Weft
@claim n > 10
@claim mean(d) (_ > 0.5) (_ < 9)
```

A failure is recorded in a block, and the filter reports it with the cell's
label. In R chunk code, `claim()` is as it always was. `claim()` given
directly to `weft_put()` is different: the check travels with the value, and
counts each time the name is used in a sentence:

```r
weft_put(worst = claim(worst, . < 50))
```

A check in the sentence is a guard around the value. `[x]{if="worst < 50"}`
that is false fails the render, as any claim does:

```markdown
The worst reading was [`worst`{.num}]{if="worst < 50"} NTU.
```

The detail line of the report names each value the guard read, as `claim()`
names its value: `worst < 50 was false (worst = 52.5)`. With two names it
reads `n_gap < n_sites was false (n_gap = 12, n_sites = 3)`.

Each failing part of a comma list is its own failure, with the names that part
read. A bool prints as `true` or `false` and a date as ISO text.

The filter does not read a `claim=` or `level=` key. On a named value or on a
span it resolves, either key is a construct error that says so, because the
check would never run. Use a guard span, or `claim()` in code. On an R value
in a knitr document, `level` passes through as it did.

`checks()` lists these guards with the rest of a project's checks, grouped
by the name they check (see `vignette("wording", package = "weft")`).

## What failure looks like

The filter does not stop at the first problem. It marks each failure in the
text with `<<weft: KIND, line N>>`, finishes, and reports once on standard
error. The kinds are `failed claim`, `no value`, `value error` and
`construct error`:

```text
weft: 1 claim failed
  survey.qmd:12  `worst`{.num}
      _ < 50 was false (value 52.5)
Read each sentence. If FALSE is right, rewrite the sentence.
Do not loosen a claim to clear this.
```

The render then fails. In draft mode it does not fail: the markers, the
report and the stamp are the same, but the exit is clean. Draft mode is on
when the environment variable `WEFT_DRAFT` is `1` or `true`, or `draft: true`
is in `_weft.yml` or the document's `weft:` key. The filter reads those two
as text, not through Pandoc's metadata. A `weft:` mapping in flow style is
read as the block form is.

Under `quarto render` in a project set up with `use_quarto()`, the report
prints once, from the post-render script, which collects every document's
failures. With plain Pandoc, or a Quarto render with no post-render script, the
filter prints it.

A failure's line is found by searching the source, its includes and its chunk
options for the construct's text. Text that a chunk printed has no line, and
the report names the file only. If a construct's text also appears later in
the source, a printed construct takes that later line. A span in a pipe-table
cell whose attribute holds `\|` is found too.

### The traps

A name published nowhere in the document:

```text
no value is published under the name `depth` in this document (rule 1.12.7).
Publish it in code in this document: weft_put(depth = ...) in R, put(depth=...) in
Python, @put depth in Julia. A cell with include: false or output: false
publishes nothing on the jupyter and julia engines.
```

A condition outside the grammar:

```text
`worst + 1 > 3` is not a name or one comparison of names, numbers and
'strings'; bind the condition to a name in code (rule 1.12.4).
```

A class the filter does not implement:

```text
`.uname` on a named value is not available in this version of weft.lua
(rule 2.13.3).
```

A hidden cell is the usual cause of the first. On the Jupyter and Julia
engines a cell with `include: false` or `output: false` publishes nothing,
because its output never reaches Pandoc. Publish in a cell that shows its
output, and use `echo: false` to hide the code.

## Values files

A pipeline can publish values for a document it never runs. Write a values
file, then read it from the document at the point where the values should
begin to count.

```r
weft_values_write("_weft/values/survey.json", n = nrow(d), worst = max(d$ntu))
```

`````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
````{.weft-values file="_weft/values/survey.json"}
````

Mean depth was `worst`{.num} NTU at `n`{.word} sites.
`````

`weft_values_write()` works outside a knit and in a `targets` pipeline. The
file is JSON, in the same form as the block. A relative path in the document
is taken from the document's folder, and a path that starts with `/` from the
project root, which is the folder with `_weft.yml`, else `_quarto.yml`, else the
document's own. The file must resolve inside the root. A `../` that stays
inside is fine. A path that leaves the root, a drive or `//` form, a missing
file, a directory, a file over 5,000,000 bytes, or a file that is not schema 1
is a failure that names the file and the reason. The size is checked before the
file is read. The filter does not follow symbolic links. A body on a `file=`
block is also a failure. The `named-unpublished` lint refuses a file outside the
root too, so it does not count the names in it.

A values file is left out of freshness. Its own run id is not compared with the
current run, so a file a pipeline wrote earlier does not make the document
"not fresh" or print the notice below.

Chapters of a book share values only by each reading the same file. The
ledger header lists each file read, by its path from the root, with its hash.

## Captions and front matter

A named value works in any caption, on any chunk, and in the front-matter
fields `title`, `subtitle`, `abstract` and `description`. The filter resolves
them after the body, so each sees the last value published under the name.

```markdown
---
title: "Turbidity at `n`{.word} sites"
---
```

## A named value in math and raw LaTeX

A named value works inside a formula and inside raw LaTeX. Pandoc keeps the
backticks in the text of a `$...$` or `$$...$$` formula, so the filter finds the
named value there, and writes the TeX that a class block writes in math (see
`vignette("values")`, "Values in math and raw LaTeX"), not markdown:

`````{verbatim, lang = "markdown"}
````{.weft-values}
{"weft":1,"values":{"share":{"t":"float","v":"0.123"},"volume":{"t":"float","v":"1234567"}}}
````

The share was $s = `share`{.pct}$ of the flow, and the volume

$$ V = `volume`{.sci} $$
`````

gives the formulas `s = 12.3\%` and `V = 1.2 \times 10^{6}`. The same holds in
a math environment such as `align` and in raw LaTeX (a `{=latex}` fence, another
`\begin{...}` environment, a code span followed by `{=latex}`), where the output
is wrapped in `\ensuremath{...}`.

The checks are those of math written with inline R: the classes that print
words, emphasis or a list are a construct error, and so is a class or key that
is not weft's. `.val` is allowed, and prints `\text{...}` for anything but a
plain number. A failure is the marker `\text{<<weft: no value, line 7>>}` inside
the formula, which is not split. The name counts in the ledger and the stamp
(context `math`, or `tex` in raw LaTeX), and a use above the publication
follows the rule of the section above. With the filter not installed, or not
run before `weft-check.lua`, a named value left in a formula is a finding of
`weft-check`: "math holds a named value the filter did not resolve".

## Freeze, kept kernels and `verify()`

A value published in an earlier render can reach a later one: a document
served from `_freeze`, a cache, or a Jupyter kernel or Julia server that
kept its state. Each publisher records a run id, from `.weft/run`, else
`WEFT_RUN`. When a block's run is not the current one, the filter prints a
notice once, to standard error. The notice fails nothing in an ordinary
render. Its checks did not run now.

`verify()` fails on it. Before rendering, `verify()` writes `.weft/run`,
restarts Jupyter kernels, and, for a document on the Julia engine, kills the
Julia server. That ends any other Julia notebook open in that server, and the
report says so.

## The lints

Three lints read named values, without rendering:

| Id | Tier | Finds | What to do |
|---|---|---|---|
| `named-unpublished` | 2 | a name used in a sentence that no executed chunk, hand-written block or values file mentions | publish it with `weft_put()`, `put()` or `@put`; the lint fires once per name, at its first use |
| `publish-hidden` | 1 | a `put`, `weft.put`, `@put` or `Weft.put` in a cell with `include: false` or `output: false`, on the Jupyter or Julia engine | publish in a cell that shows its output |
| `publish-hidden-auto` | 2 | the same, for `auto()` | the same, or call `auto()` in a shown cell |

`publish-hidden` also fires on a hidden cell that assigns a name the prose uses,
in a document that calls `auto()`. Without the lint the render would print an
earlier value of that name with no error: see Limits.

A name can come from a helper script or a `from helpers import *`, which a
search cannot see. That is why `named-unpublished` is tier 2: the render still
fails loudly if the name is missing.

The `engine` rule accepts a `.qmd` with no `engine: knitr` when every construct
in it is a named value or a span in the filter's grammar, and the filter is
installed. It still stops one that holds an R value, or a span outside the
grammar, and its hint now says to write each value as a name. A document with
named values and no filter installed is a finding of its own: run
`use_quarto()`.

The gate counts a named value as a value, and `claim(` in a Python chunk and
`@claim` in a Julia chunk as claim calls. A hand-written block and a values
file are not counted.

## Limits

- On the Jupyter engine, `auto()` cannot know that a hidden cell's output was
  dropped. If a cell with `include: false` or `output: false` changes a name
  that an earlier cell published, the prose keeps the earlier value, with no
  error. The `publish-hidden` lint finds the cell; publish in a cell that shows
  its output.
- A construct's line is the next occurrence of its text. Text printed by a
  chunk that also appears later in the source takes the later line.
- Julia has no `auto()`, and neither language has a `checked()` that makes a
  check count where the name is used. `claim()` from Python and Julia is
  checked where it runs.
- Units, the dictionary and project formatters stay in R.
- The filter does not follow symbolic links when it reads a values file.
- Inline R used above the code that defines its value is not resolved
  later; only a named value is.
- Tables in a Jupyter or Julia document are recorded in the ledger by the
  filter, with the limits in the languages article. A table that a script
  fills in after the page loads is recorded by the HTML it holds.
- A guest `claim` counts in the commit gate only in an executed chunk, so
  turning `eval` off on a Python chunk with a claim reads as a removal.
- `.sci` prints some whole mantissas inconsistently (`1 x 10^10` but
  `1.0 x 10^6`), and `.pct` of a value near 1e15 rounds one digit early.
- The Jupyter and Julia engines run on the author's machine only. The CI job
  that `use_ci()` writes runs the static checks, and installs no Quarto,
  Jupyter or Julia.
- The Julia package is installed from git. Nothing is published to PyPI or a
  Julia registry.
